takeaways: The price of one bitcoin is not the price of getting started.
Bitcoin divides into decimals: spend 100 at 50,000 and you hold 0.002 BTC.
Each platform sets its own minimum order and fees, so check both first.

quiz.q: One bitcoin is 50,000 USDT. You spend 100 USDT, ignoring fees. What do you get?
options: Nothing, you need a whole coin
0.02 BTC
quiz.why: 100 ÷ 50,000 = 0.002. You can hold a fraction of one bitcoin.

takeaways: USDT is a stablecoin designed to stay close to one dollar, not a bank deposit.
Exchanges use it to price and swap assets, so a sale often ends in USDT.
"Stable" is a design goal: the price can drift and redemption has conditions.

quiz.q: Which statement about USDT is true?
options: It is the dollars in your bank account
It is a stablecoin, a type of crypto asset
It can never move away from one dollar
quiz.why: USDT aims to track the dollar, but it is a crypto asset with its own issuer and platform risks.

takeaways: On an exchange account, the platform mainly manages the assets and keys.
In a self-custody wallet you control the credentials, and the recovery duty is yours.
Ask who controls the permission to move the assets before you choose.

quiz.q: You lose the recovery phrase of a standard self-custody wallet and have no other recovery method. What happens?
options: Support can reset it for you
Access may be lost for good
The exchange restores it automatically
quiz.why: With self-custody you hold the keys. Without the phrase or another valid method, nobody can recover it for you.

takeaways: Check that the platform serves your real country before anything else.
Sign up only through the confirmed official entry, with your own email or phone.
Right after sign-up, turn on security features and save your recovery options.

quiz.q: What should you confirm first, before signing up?
options: The size of the welcome reward
That the platform serves your country and the entry is official
How many followers the platform has
quiz.why: Eligibility and the official entry come first. A reward should never decide where you open an account.

takeaways: KYC confirms you are the account owner and helps the platform meet the rules.
Submit your ID only inside the official verification flow, never in a chat.
If it fails, read the reason, fix it and try again with your real identity.

quiz.q: Who should receive your ID?
options: A helpful "agent" in a chat group
Only the verified official verification flow
The course chat, so others can check it
quiz.why: Only the official flow. NexuAlpha never asks for your ID, and neither should a stranger.

takeaways: A fiat deposit, buying crypto, an on-chain deposit and an internal transfer are different routes.
On-chain deposits need a supported coin and network; internal transfers stay on the platform.
Never pay a stranger off-platform; check where the balance will land first.

quiz.q: You move USDT from your funding account to your trading account on the same platform. What is that?
options: An on-chain deposit
An internal transfer
A fiat deposit
quiz.why: It only moves balance between your own accounts. It is usually not an on-chain transfer.

takeaways: BTC/USDT means bitcoin priced in USDT: you pay USDT and receive bitcoin.
Check whether the order box wants an amount of money or a number of coins.
After you buy, check the trade record: fill status, average price and fee.

quiz.q: You buy 0.002 BTC at 50,000 with a 0.1% fee taken separately in USDT. What is the total spent?
quiz.why: 100 for the coins plus a 0.10 fee makes 100.10.

takeaways: Selling for USDT gives you a USDT balance, not money in your bank.
Selling and withdrawing to your bank are two separate steps.
A higher price is not your net gain: subtract every fee first.

quiz.q: You sold your bitcoin for USDT. Where is the money now?
options: In your bank account
As a USDT balance on the platform
Already converted to your local currency
quiz.why: You received USDT. Getting money to your bank is a separate withdrawal step.

takeaways: Confirm the coin and the network the receiver supports before you send.
Copy the address from the receiving page, check all of it and add any memo or tag.
Send a small test first and confirm it was credited.

quiz.q: The receiving page asks for a memo. What do you do?
options: Skip it, the address is enough
Fill in the memo exactly as shown
Use the memo from an old transfer
quiz.why: If a memo or tag is required, the transfer may not be credited without it.

takeaways: Submitted, on-chain and credited are three different stations.
Use the transaction hash on a block explorer for the right network.
Share records with official support, never your recovery phrase, private key or codes.

quiz.q: Your transfer says "sent" but has not arrived. What is the first step?
options: Send the same amount again
Find where it is stuck using the record and transaction hash
Pay someone who promises to recover it
quiz.why: Find the station first, then contact the matching official channel. Do not keep sending.

takeaways: Your recovery phrase and private key are control keys, not support codes.
Guaranteed returns and pressure to pay are danger signs.
Never confirm a signature or approval you do not understand.

quiz.q: Which one is safe to share so you can receive a payment?
options: Your public address
Your recovery phrase
A one-time code
quiz.why: A public address is made for receiving. Secrets and codes give control away.

takeaways: A correct flow is the goal: entry and eligibility, spot, amount and fee, then the record.
Stopping an unclear transfer is a correct answer too.
Your certificate is a learning record, not a licence to invest.

quiz.q: A practice transfer shows the wrong network. What is the right move?
options: Send it anyway and hope
Stop and do not send
Switch to a bigger amount
quiz.why: When the network, fees or identity are unclear, stopping matters more than finishing the task.

takeaways: The last price is the most recent trade, not an offer for any size.
Larger orders can fill across several levels of the order book.
Slippage and the trading fee are separate costs: check the bill.

quiz.q: Half of your 0.002 BTC fills at 50,000 and the other half at 50,100. What is your average price?
quiz.why: Two equal halves average to 50,050. The fee is a separate cost on top.

takeaways: A market order fills fast at the prices available now; the final price can move.
A limit order caps your price, but it may not fill.
Cancel only affects the unfilled part; what already filled stays.

quiz.q: Your limit order is half filled and you cancel it. What happens?
options: Everything is reversed
Only the unfilled half is cancelled
The filled half turns into a market order
quiz.why: A cancel cannot rewind a fill. It only stops the remaining quantity.

takeaways: One candle shows four prices for one period: open, high, low and close.
Read the time frame before the shape: five minutes is not a day.
Colours differ between apps, and one candle is a record, not a prediction.

quiz.q: A five-minute candle opens at 50,000, reaches 51,000, dips to 49,000 and closes at 50,500. What is the high?
quiz.why: The top of the upper wick is the highest price in that period: 51,000.

takeaways: Account balance, position size and planned risk are three different numbers.
Decide your exit first, then size the position.
With a 5% stop and a 20 risk budget, the position is about 400.

quiz.q: Entry 50,000, planned exit 47,500, and you accept losing 20. About how big is the position?
quiz.why: The exit is 5% away, and 5% of 400 is 20. Costs come on top.

takeaways: A stop-loss runs your exit plan; it is not insurance.
A stop-market exits fast but can slip in a fast market.
A stop-limit caps the price but may not fill at all.

quiz.q: In a sharp drop, what can happen to a stop-limit order?
options: It always fills at the trigger price
It may not fill if the price races past
It turns into insurance
quiz.why: The limit protects your price, so the order can stay unfilled when the market moves fast.

takeaways: Spot swaps one asset for another; a perpetual is a contract position.
Long gains if the price rises, short gains if it falls; the wrong side loses.
Futures are a different risk structure, not a level you must reach.

quiz.q: Does a futures position give you bitcoin you can withdraw?
options: Yes, it is the same as spot
No, it is a contract that settles profit and loss
Only with 10x leverage
quiz.why: A linear perpetual settles profit and loss in the contract. It is not a withdrawable coin balance.

takeaways: 100 of margin controlling a 1,000 position is 10x leverage.
Price moves act on the position, and your margin takes the result.
With the same position size, changing leverage changes the margin, not the P&L.

quiz.q: A 1,000 position moves 1% against you, ignoring fees. About how much do you lose?
quiz.why: 1% of the 1,000 position is about 10, taken from your margin.

takeaways: Initial margin opens a position; maintenance margin keeps it open.
Equity is margin plus or minus the open result: 100 down 20 leaves 80.
The risk system can step in before your margin reaches zero.

quiz.q: Initial margin is 100 and the position is down 20, ignoring fees. What is the simplified equity?
quiz.why: 100 minus the 20 loss leaves 80, and the buffer keeps shrinking if the price moves further against you.

takeaways: Isolated margin gives one position its own margin.
The margin you assigned can still be lost; isolated is not a stop-loss.
Auto-add or manual adding puts more of your money behind the same risk.

quiz.q: You turn on auto-add margin for an isolated position. What changes?
options: Nothing, the loss stays capped at the first 100
More of your balance can flow into the position
The position becomes risk-free
quiz.why: Auto-add moves available balance into the position, so more money carries the risk.

takeaways: Cross margin shares one margin pool across positions.
One losing position can eat the buffer the others rely on.
It does not reach your bank cards or personal wallets.

quiz.q: Is cross margin automatically safer?
options: Yes, it can never be liquidated
Not necessarily, it depends on the shared pool and the rules
Yes, it uses all your bank cards
quiz.why: Extra margin can delay risk handling, but it also puts more of your money on the line.

takeaways: Many perpetuals judge liquidation by the mark price and margin rules, not the last trade.
Near the maintenance requirement, the system can reduce or close the position.
A closed position does not come back when the price rebounds.

quiz.q: A leveraged position was liquidated, and later the price went back up. What happens?
options: The position comes back on its own
It stays closed; the path mattered
The exchange refunds the loss
quiz.why: Once force-closed, the position is gone. A later rebound only helps someone still holding.

takeaways: Funding is paid between longs and shorts, not a fixed charge to the exchange.
It is based on the position value: 1,000 at 0.01% is 0.10.
Choosing not to trade is a passing answer too.

quiz.q: The funding rate is positive. Who usually pays?
options: Shorts pay longs
Longs pay shorts
Everyone pays the exchange
quiz.why: With a positive rate, longs usually pay shorts. With a negative rate it flips.
